questions.stem: This illustration shows the procedure essential for confirming ALL when blood counts are abnormal. In an adult, from which site is the needle most commonly inserted?

explanation.summary: Bone marrow biopsy/aspiration in adults is most safely and commonly performed at the posterior superior iliac crest to sample marrow for blasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow biopsy/aspiration in adults is most safely and commonly performed at the posterior superior iliac crest to sample marrow for blasts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The distal femur is not a standard marrow biopsy site in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The proximal tibia is used for marrow access in infants and for intraosseous lines, but not routinely for adult marrow biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sternum may be used for aspiration only (not core biopsy) and carries risk of mediastinal injury, so it is not the most common site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lumbar spinous process is not used; lumbar puncture samples CSF between vertebrae, not bone marrow.

questions.stem: The left chest radiograph from a child with T-cell ALL differs from the normal film on the right at the arrow. What abnormality does the arrow indicate?

explanation.summary: T-cell ALL commonly presents with an anterior mediastinal mass from lymphadenopathy, seen here as widening/opacity absent on the normal comparison film.
explanation.whyCorrect: T-cell ALL commonly presents with an anterior mediastinal mass from lymphadenopathy, seen here as widening/opacity absent on the normal comparison film.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tension pneumothorax shows a hyperlucent hemithorax without lung markings and mediastinal shift away from the affected side, not mediastinal widening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiomegaly enlarges the cardiac silhouette below, whereas T-ALL characteristically widens the upper anterior mediastinum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lobar pneumonia appears as consolidation within lung parenchyma with air bronchograms, not a central mediastinal opacity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A large pleural effusion blunts the costophrenic angle with a meniscus at the lung base, not widening of the central mediastinum.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear shows an increased number of the arrowed cells, all with normal nuclear segmentation of 2 to 5 lobes. What is the most common underlying cause of this finding?

explanation.summary: The cells are mature segmented neutrophils, consistent with benign mature neutrophilia. This most commonly occurs as a reactive response to bacterial infection or inflammation (also stress, smoking, and corticosteroids).
explanation.whyCorrect: The cells are mature segmented neutrophils, consistent with benign mature neutrophilia. This most commonly occurs as a reactive response to bacterial infection or inflammation (also stress, smoking, and corticosteroids).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron deficiency affects red cells and does not cause an increase in mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B12 deficiency causes hypersegmented neutrophils with six or more lobes, not more neutrophils with normal 2-to-5-lobe nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral infections typically raise lymphocytes, including reactive lymphocytes, rather than mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ALL fills the blood with lymphoblasts and often causes neutropenia, not an increase of mature segmented neutrophils.

questions.stem: The neutrophil at the center of this smear contains prominent dark primary granules that stain nearly the same color as its nucleus. What does this toxic change most commonly indicate?

explanation.summary: This is toxic granulation, an increase in darkly staining primary granules. It is a toxic change seen with bacterial infections and inflammation, reflecting activated neutrophil production.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is toxic granulation, an increase in darkly staining primary granules. It is a toxic change seen with bacterial infections and inflammation, reflecting activated neutrophil production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CML shows a full spectrum of granulocyte precursors and basophilia; toxic granulation is a reactive change of infection or inflammation, not CML's hallmark.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parasitic infections typically cause eosinophilia, not toxic granulation of neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Allergic reactions increase eosinophils, which have large orange-red granules, not dark primary granules in neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Megaloblastic anemia causes hypersegmented neutrophils from impaired DNA synthesis, not toxic granulation.

questions.stem: This neutrophil shows small clear bubbles in its cytoplasm in addition to coarse toxic granules. What process produces these vacuoles?

explanation.summary: Cytoplasmic vacuolization results from degranulation of lysosomes within neutrophils, usually during widespread destruction of pathogens. It is most often seen in sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytoplasmic vacuolization results from degranulation of lysosomes within neutrophils, usually during widespread destruction of pathogens. It is most often seen in sepsis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Apoptosis condenses and fragments the nucleus (karyorrhexis); it does not create clear cytoplasmic bubbles alongside toxic granules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperlipidemia does not produce cytoplasmic vacuoles in neutrophils; these form from lysosomal degranulation during phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Viral inclusions are dense bodies in infected tissue cells, such as owl-eye CMV inclusions, not clear vacuoles in neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemosiderin is golden-brown iron pigment in macrophages, not clear vacuoles in neutrophils.

questions.stem: The arrow points to a small pale blue-gray inclusion at the periphery of this neutrophil's cytoplasm. What is this structure composed of?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanation.summary: This is a Dohle body, a peripheral blue-gray cytoplasmic inclusion made of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum. It reflects increased protein production in neutrophils responding to bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a Dohle body, a peripheral blue-gray cytoplasmic inclusion made of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum. It reflects increased protein production in neutrophils responding to bacterial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Phagocytosed bacteria appear as small dark rods or cocci inside vacuoles, not as a pale blue-gray patch at the cell edge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils retain their nucleus; DNA remnants such as Howell-Jolly bodies are dense purple dots in red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aggregated hemoglobin (Heinz bodies) forms in red cells under oxidative stress, not in neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitochondria are not visible as discrete inclusions on Wright stain; the blue color reflects ribosomal RNA.

questions.stem: This figure compares lymphocyte morphology: cell A appears small and normal, while cells B and C are larger, with more abundant and irregular cytoplasm. What term best describes cells B and C?

explanation.summary: Cells B and C show the enlarged, voluminous, sometimes deeply basophilic cytoplasm of reactive lymphocytes, typically seen in viral infections, as opposed to the small mature lymphocyte in A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cells B and C show the enlarged, voluminous, sometimes deeply basophilic cytoplasm of reactive lymphocytes, typically seen in viral infections, as opposed to the small mature lymphocyte in A.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasma cells have an eccentric round nucleus with clock-face chromatin and a perinuclear clear zone (hof), rather than the abundant, irregular cytoplasm shown.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blasts have a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, and nucleoli, with only a thin rim of cytoplasm, not abundant cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smudge cells are crushed lymphocytes without intact cytoplasm, typical of CLL, not intact large cells with irregular cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulocytes have lobulated nuclei and cytoplasmic granules, whereas these are lymphocytes with round nuclei and agranular cytoplasm.

questions.stem: This smear shows enlarged lymphocytes with abundant, deeply basophilic cytoplasm that molds around neighboring red cells. This reactive appearance is most characteristic of which category of illness?

explanation.summary: These are reactive lymphocytes, larger than normal with voluminous, deeply basophilic cytoplasm. They are classically produced by viral infections, especially infectious mononucleosis (EBV).
explanation.whyCorrect: These are reactive lymphocytes, larger than normal with voluminous, deeply basophilic cytoplasm. They are classically produced by viral infections, especially infectious mononucleosis (EBV).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency anemia affects red cells (microcytosis, hypochromia) and does not produce reactive lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Allergic drug reactions classically cause eosinophilia; reactive lymphocytes are not the typical finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CML shows increased granulocytes at all stages of maturation and basophilia, not reactive lymphocytes molding around red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacterial pneumonia usually causes neutrophilia with left shift and toxic changes, not reactive lymphocytes.

questions.stem: This large lymphocyte has abundant pale cytoplasm that abuts and molds around the adjacent red blood cells, giving a 'fried egg' appearance. It is most classically associated with which virus?

explanation.summary: This is a Downey type II cell, a reactive lymphocyte with abundant agranular cytoplasm that molds around neighboring erythrocytes. It is the most common reactive lymphocyte and is classically associated with Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a Downey type II cell, a reactive lymphocyte with abundant agranular cytoplasm that molds around neighboring erythrocytes. It is the most common reactive lymphocyte and is classically associated with Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis C causes chronic liver disease and is not the classic cause of Downey cells molding around red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza may cause mild lymphocyte changes but is not classically associated with prominent reactive lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV seroconversion can produce some reactive lymphocytes, but the classic association with these molding lymphocytes is infectious mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CMV causes a heterophile-negative mononucleosis with reactive lymphocytes, but EBV is the most classic cause.

questions.stem: In the deep cortical region of the lymph node labeled the paracortex in this diagram, which lymphocyte population predominates?

explanation.summary: The paracortex (deep cortex) is the T-cell zone of the lymph node, whereas the follicles of the outer cortex contain predominantly B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The paracortex (deep cortex) is the T-cell zone of the lymph node, whereas the follicles of the outer cortex contain predominantly B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasma cells mostly reside in the medullary cords, where they secrete antibodies, not the paracortex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages are concentrated in the medullary sinuses and germinal centers (tingible-body macrophages), not dominating the paracortex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B cells populate the follicles and germinal centers of the outer cortex, not the deep cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells are found mainly in blood and spleen and do not form a distinct lymph node zone.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph shows symmetric enlargement of both hilar regions (arrows) in a young adult. Which condition is the most likely underlying cause of this pattern?

explanation.summary: Bilateral, symmetric hilar lymphadenopathy in a young adult is the classic radiographic finding of the granulomatous disease sarcoidosis. Malignancies and infections more often cause asymmetric or unilateral adenopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bilateral, symmetric hilar lymphadenopathy in a young adult is the classic radiographic finding of the granulomatous disease sarcoidosis. Malignancies and infections more often cause asymmetric or unilateral adenopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents with an anterior mediastinal mass and often asymmetric nodes, rather than symmetric bilateral hilar enlargement alone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary tuberculosis tends to cause unilateral hilar adenopathy with a Ghon focus, not symmetric bilateral hilar enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bronchogenic carcinoma usually causes a lung mass with unilateral, ipsilateral hilar adenopathy, and is unusual in young adults.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histoplasmosis can cause hilar adenopathy, but it is often asymmetric with calcified granulomas and a history of bird or bat dropping exposure.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This stained smear shows bacilli with a 'safety-pin' appearance (arrow). What staining feature produces this look?

explanation.summary: Y. pestis characteristically shows bipolar (dye taken up preferentially at each end) staining with stains such as Wright/Giemsa, giving a closed-safety-pin appearance useful in identification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis characteristically shows bipolar (dye taken up preferentially at each end) staining with stains such as Wright/Giemsa, giving a closed-safety-pin appearance useful in identification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central endospores create an unstained gap in rods such as Clostridium or Bacillus, but Yersinia pestis does not form spores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies are features of viruses or chlamydia within host cells, not of free-living bacilli.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A capsular halo appears as a clear zone around the organism on negative staining, not as dense dye at both poles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metachromatic volutin granules are characteristic of Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which appear as club-shaped rods, not safety pins.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This CDC map plots reported human cases concentrated in the western United States. Which zoonotic infection is being mapped?

explanation.summary: Plague is endemic in the rural western US, where rodents, prairie dogs, and their fleas maintain the reservoir; only a handful of human cases (0-17) occur annually, clustered in these western states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plague is endemic in the rural western US, where rodents, prairie dogs, and their fleas maintain the reservoir; only a handful of human cases (0-17) occur annually, clustered in these western states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tularemia cases concentrate in the south-central states, especially Arkansas and Missouri, not the Southwest and Pacific states.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ehrlichiosis is tick-borne (lone star tick) and concentrated in the south-central and southeastern United States, not the rural West.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, despite its name, is most common in the southeastern and south-central states such as North Carolina, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lyme disease is concentrated in the Northeast and upper Midwest, with very few cases in the western states.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This markedly enlarged, tender lymph node in a febrile patient is the defining lesion of which form of plague?

explanation.summary: A bubo is a massively enlarged, painful regional lymph node draining the site of an infected flea bite; it defines bubonic plague, the most common (80-90%) form of Y. pestis infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bubo is a massively enlarged, painful regional lymph node draining the site of an infected flea bite; it defines bubonic plague, the most common (80-90%) form of Y. pestis infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacillary angiomatosis is a Bartonella infection in immunocompromised hosts, producing vascular skin nodules rather than a single huge tender node.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumonic plague is a fulminant lung infection with bloody sputum, often spread person-to-person; it is not defined by a regional bubo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Septicemic plague is bacteremia without a prominent bubo, presenting with shock and DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ulceroglandular tularemia also causes regional lymphadenopathy, but it has an ulcer at the inoculation site and is not a form of plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This blackened, gangrenous necrosis of the fingers in a septic patient reflects which underlying process that gave plague its 'Black Death' nickname?

explanation.summary: In septicemic plague, systemic inflammation triggers DIC, shock, and microvascular thrombosis, producing acral (fingertip/extremity) ischemic necrosis and gangrene, the classic 'Black Death' appearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: In septicemic plague, systemic inflammation triggers DIC, shock, and microvascular thrombosis, producing acral (fingertip/extremity) ischemic necrosis and gangrene, the classic 'Black Death' appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Y. pestis does not cause gangrene through a direct dermonecrotic exotoxin; the necrosis is ischemic from widespread microvascular thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis causes palpable purpura, not symmetric acral gangrene from microvascular thrombosis in septic shock.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Superficial thrombophlebitis causes tender, cordlike veins, not blackened, necrotic fingertips.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A flea-bite reaction stays at the bite site and is mild; it cannot produce gangrene of multiple fingers.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This map shows US cases of a rabbit-associated zoonosis clustered in the Ozarks. How is this organism usually transmitted to humans?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite of an infected rat flea

explanation.summary: Francisella tularensis (rabbit fever) is transmitted by handling infected rabbits or by arthropod vectors (ticks, deer flies); US cases concentrate in the Ozarks (Missouri and Arkansas).
explanation.whyCorrect: Francisella tularensis (rabbit fever) is transmitted by handling infected rabbits or by arthropod vectors (ticks, deer flies); US cases concentrate in the Ozarks (Missouri and Arkansas).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rat flea bites transmit plague (Yersinia pestis), not the rabbit-associated infection tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Contaminated water is an uncommon route for tularemia; the usual exposure is handling infected animals or arthropod bites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cat scratches transmit Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease), not Francisella tularensis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tularemia is not spread from person to person, which is notable given that it is highly infectious.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This punched-out ulcer at an inoculation site, with regional lymphadenopathy in a rabbit hunter, is characteristic of which condition?

explanation.summary: Ulceroglandular tularemia (75-85% of cases) uniquely ulcerates at the inoculation site along with enlarged local lymph nodes, fever, chills, and malaise, distinguishing it from the non-ulcerating bubo of plague.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulceroglandular tularemia (75-85% of cases) uniquely ulcerates at the inoculation site along with enlarged local lymph nodes, fever, chills, and malaise, distinguishing it from the non-ulcerating bubo of plague.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bubonic plague causes a painful, swollen bubo without an ulcer at the bite site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cat scratch disease begins with a small papule or pustule after cat contact, not a punched-out ulcer after rabbit hunting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A syphilitic chancre is a painless, clean-based genital ulcer from sexual contact, unrelated to rabbit exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cutaneous anthrax forms a painless black eschar surrounded by edema, typically from contact with livestock hides or wool.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This crusted primary inoculation papule with adjacent lymphadenitis on the neck of a young child with cat exposure is most consistent with which infection?

explanation.summary: A crusted inoculation papule with adjacent regional lymphadenitis in a child who has contact with cats and multiple scratches is the classic presentation of cat scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae.
explanation.whyCorrect: A crusted inoculation papule with adjacent regional lymphadenitis in a child who has contact with cats and multiple scratches is the classic presentation of cat scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Impetigo shows honey-colored crusts on the face and does not usually come with prominent regional lymphadenitis after cat contact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kawasaki disease causes fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, and extremity changes, not an inoculation papule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ulceroglandular tularemia follows rabbit or tick exposure and forms an ulcer, not a crusted papule after cat scratches.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scrofula is mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis without a cat-related inoculation papule.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: These multiple red-purple vascular skin nodules in a severely immunocompromised transplant recipient, caused by a gram-negative bacillus, represent which condition?

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4, transplant, chemotherapy) and produces friable, bright red-purple vascular nodules; unlike the histologically similar Kaposi sarcoma, its lesions bleed easily and show neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4, transplant, chemotherapy) and produces friable, bright red-purple vascular nodules; unlike the histologically similar Kaposi sarcoma, its lesions bleed easily and show neutrophilic infiltrates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metastatic carcinoma produces firm skin nodules from tumor cells, not infection by a gram-negative bacillus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and shows lymphocytic, not neutrophilic, infiltrates; it is a viral neoplasm rather than a bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyogenic granulomas are usually single, rapidly growing benign lesions often after trauma, not multiple infectious nodules in immunocompromise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Disseminated candidiasis produces papulopustular lesions from a fungus, not friable vascular nodules from a gram-negative bacillus.

questions.stem: This Giemsa-stained thick blood smear shows an elongated, sheathed larval organism coiling among the red cells. What is this organism?

explanation.summary: Microfilariae of W. bancrofti are small larval nematodes seen in thick blood smears stained with Giemsa; they circulate in the blood with nocturnal periodicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microfilariae of W. bancrofti are small larval nematodes seen in thick blood smears stained with Giemsa; they circulate in the blood with nocturnal periodicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trypanosoma brucei trypomastigotes are smaller and have an undulating membrane and flagellum, not a coiled sheathed larva.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loa loa adults live in subcutaneous tissue and migrate across the eye; they are not seen in blood smears.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. falciparum gametocytes are banana-shaped and sit within red cells, not large free larvae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Borrelia recurrentis is a thin spirochete that is much smaller and lacks a sheath.

questions.stem: This Giemsa-stained thick blood smear from a febrile traveler shows a long, coiled, sheathed larva among the red cells. Detection of this organism confirms infection with which parasite?

explanation.summary: A peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa demonstrating sheathed microfilariae is the most straightforward way to identify W. bancrofti.
explanation.whyCorrect: A peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa demonstrating sheathed microfilariae is the most straightforward way to identify W. bancrofti.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasmodium falciparum appears as small rings and banana-shaped gametocytes within red cells, not a long sheathed larva.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Babesia appears as intraerythrocytic rings and tetrad (Maltese cross) forms, not free larvae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira are thin spirochetes not visible on routine Giemsa smears; they are diagnosed by serology or PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trypanosoma cruzi appears as C-shaped trypomastigotes with a kinetoplast and flagellum, not sheathed larvae.

questions.stem: This thick blood smear stained with Giemsa demonstrates a single elongated sheathed microfilaria. Given this organism's periodicity, when should the blood sample ideally be collected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early in the morning at waking

choices.label: C
choices.text: At night, around 10 PM to 2 AM

choices.label: D
choices.text: At any random time of day

explanation.summary: W. bancrofti microfilariae are nocturnal, so blood collected at night (approximately 10 PM to 2 AM) yields the highest diagnostic sensitivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: W. bancrofti microfilariae are nocturnal, so blood collected at night (approximately 10 PM to 2 AM) yields the highest diagnostic sensitivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early morning collection misses the nocturnal peak, since microfilariae retreat to the lungs during the day.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fatty meal makes plasma lipemic but does not increase W. bancrofti microfilariae in the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Because W. bancrofti shows strong nocturnal periodicity, random daytime sampling often yields false negatives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Midday sampling is ideal for day-biting Loa loa, not for nocturnally periodic W. bancrofti.

questions.stem: Panel (a) shows marked conjunctival redness without purulent discharge and panel (b) shows oral mucosal hemorrhage in a systemically ill patient. These findings are most characteristic of severe disease caused by which organism?

explanation.summary: Conjunctival suffusion is a hallmark of leptospirosis, and severe (Weil) disease can produce hemorrhage such as the oral bleeding shown here.
explanation.whyCorrect: Conjunctival suffusion is a hallmark of leptospirosis, and severe (Weil) disease can produce hemorrhage such as the oral bleeding shown here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Yellow fever causes jaundice and hemorrhage but is not characterized by conjunctival suffusion without discharge.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dengue causes fever, retro-orbital pain, rash, and possible hemorrhage, but conjunctival suffusion is not its hallmark.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is typified by a rash spreading from wrists and ankles toward the trunk after a tick bite, not conjunctival suffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: W. bancrofti causes lymphatic filariasis with lymphedema, not acute conjunctival suffusion and mucosal hemorrhage.

questions.stem: This patient shows gross enlargement, hyperkeratosis, and thickening of the lower leg due to long-standing lymphatic obstruction. What is the most likely underlying infection?

explanation.summary: Advanced elephantiasis of the limb reflects irreversible lymphatic fibrosis and destruction from chronic W. bancrofti infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Advanced elephantiasis of the limb reflects irreversible lymphatic fibrosis and destruction from chronic W. bancrofti infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Onchocerca volvulus causes river blindness and itchy dermatitis, not massive lymphatic leg swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leptospira causes an acute febrile illness with conjunctival suffusion and possibly Weil disease, not chronic lymphatic obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loa loa causes transient Calabar swellings and eye-worm migration, not chronic elephantiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Schistosoma mansoni causes hepatic periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension, not lymphatic obstruction of the leg.

questions.stem: This patient developed the oral findings shown after starting chemotherapy. What underlying mechanism best explains why the oral mucosa is affected?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A direct chemical burn from the drug contacting the mouth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the salivary glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: A nutritional vitamin deficiency from poor oral intake

explanation.summary: Alkylating agents kill all rapidly dividing cells, including the oral and gastric mucosa, producing mucositis and ulceration; the injured mucosa and reduced flow give the thick, pasty saliva seen here.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alkylating agents kill all rapidly dividing cells, including the oral and gastric mucosa, producing mucositis and ulceration; the injured mucosa and reduced flow give the thick, pasty saliva seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secondary infection can complicate mucositis, but the primary injury is drug killing of rapidly dividing epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Most chemotherapy is given systemically; mucosal injury reflects systemic cytotoxicity, not contact burns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune salivary gland destruction is Sjogren syndrome, not a consequence of starting chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Poor intake can worsen nutrition over time, but acute mucositis comes from direct cytotoxicity to dividing mucosal cells.

questions.stem: This chemical schematic shows mechlorethamine reacting with guanine bases located on adjacent DNA strands. What class of DNA lesion is being formed?

explanation.summary: Nitrogen mustards such as mechlorethamine are bifunctional and covalently bridge the N-7 of guanine on two opposing strands, producing an interstrand cross-link that blocks strand separation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrogen mustards such as mechlorethamine are bifunctional and covalently bridge the N-7 of guanine on two opposing strands, producing an interstrand cross-link that blocks strand separation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thymine dimers form from UV light linking adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand, not from nitrogen mustards bridging opposite strands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Depurination removes a base to leave an abasic site; the figure shows covalent bridging between two guanines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single-strand nick is a break in the backbone, typical of topoisomerase I or ionizing radiation, not a covalent bridge between strands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Base mismatches arise from replication errors and are fixed by mismatch repair; they do not covalently link two strands.

questions.stem: This figure links specific chemotherapy agents to their characteristic organ toxicities. Cyclophosphamide is mapped to the bladder; which urinary metabolite is directly responsible for that toxicity?

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide metabolism produces acrolein, which concentrates in the bladder and causes hemorrhagic cystitis; mesna binds and neutralizes acrolein to prevent this.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cyclophosphamide metabolism produces acrolein, which concentrates in the bladder and causes hemorrhagic cystitis; mesna binds and neutralizes acrolein to prevent this.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetaldehyde is the toxic metabolite of ethanol, not of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cisplatin is a separate platinum drug whose main toxicity is nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, not a metabolite of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphoramide mustard is cyclophosphamide's active alkylating metabolite responsible for its anticancer effect, not its bladder toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mesna is the protective drug that neutralizes acrolein in the bladder; it prevents rather than causes hemorrhagic cystitis.

questions.stem: This illustration shows an alkylating agent modifying DNA across three sequential panels. What is the ultimate cellular consequence depicted by the fragmented strand in the final panel?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzymatic reversal of the alkyl adducts by a methyltransferase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased transcription of DNA repair genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restoration of normal complementary base pairing

choices.label: E
choices.text: DNA strand breakage that suppresses replication and triggers apoptosis

explanation.summary: Cross-linked DNA cannot separate for replication; the cross-linked strands eventually break and replication is suppressed, arresting the cell cycle and driving the cell to apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cross-linked DNA cannot separate for replication; the cross-linked strands eventually break and replication is suppressed, arresting the cell cycle and driving the cell to apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alkylating damage degrades DNA integrity and causes mutations; it does not improve polymerase fidelity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methyltransferases such as MGMT can repair some adducts, but the fragmented strand shows unrepaired damage leading to breakage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The final panel depicts strand fragmentation and cell death, not increased expression of repair genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alkylation disrupts normal base pairing, and the broken strand shows damage rather than restoration.

questions.stem: In this diagram of where chemotherapy drug classes act across the cell cycle, why are the antimetabolite agents positioned to act specifically during the highlighted synthesis phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block mitotic spindle assembly, which occurs during the S phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: They crosslink DNA in a cell-cycle-independent manner concentrated in the S phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: They interfere with nucleotide/DNA synthesis, which only occurs during the S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: They arrest cells at the G1/S checkpoint before DNA is copied

choices.label: E
choices.text: They inhibit topoisomerase-mediated transcription unique to the S phase

explanation.summary: Antimetabolites are decoys for metabolic intermediates of DNA synthesis, so they are effective only during the S (synthesis) phase when DNA is being replicated; agents like alkylators act independent of cell-cycle phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antimetabolites are decoys for metabolic intermediates of DNA synthesis, so they are effective only during the S (synthesis) phase when DNA is being replicated; agents like alkylators act independent of cell-cycle phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spindle assembly occurs in M phase and is targeted by vinca alkaloids and taxanes, not antimetabolites.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crosslinking DNA is the mechanism of alkylating agents, which act independent of cell-cycle phase, not of antimetabolites.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antimetabolites act while DNA is being synthesized in S phase rather than by holding cells at the G1/S checkpoint.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topoisomerase inhibitors such as etoposide and irinotecan are a separate class, and topoisomerases act in replication and transcription, not uniquely in S phase.

questions.stem: This diagram maps the folate cycle that produces thymidine. What is the direct downstream consequence of the drug-mediated enzyme inhibition shown blocking dihydrofolate reductase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tetrahydrofolate cannot be regenerated, so dUMP is no longer converted to dTMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: dTMP accumulates and feedback-inhibits thymidylate synthase to protect the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess tetrahydrofolate is shunted into increased purine synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: dUMP and dTMP become covalently crosslinked within the DNA strand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymidylate synthase is activated to bypass the folate requirement

explanation.summary: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase prevents regeneration of tetrahydrofolate, the cofactor thymidylate synthase needs to methylate dUMP into dTMP; without dTMP, DNA replication in dividing cells fails.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase prevents regeneration of tetrahydrofolate, the cofactor thymidylate synthase needs to methylate dUMP into dTMP; without dTMP, DNA replication in dividing cells fails.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking DHFR depletes dTMP rather than causing it to accumulate, so there is no protective feedback.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DHFR inhibition depletes tetrahydrofolate, so it cannot be shunted into extra purine synthesis; purine synthesis also falls.
whyWrongByChoice.D: dUMP and dTMP are nucleotides, not crosslinked DNA elements; the problem is failure to make dTMP for DNA synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thymidylate synthase requires methylene-tetrahydrofolate and cannot bypass the folate requirement when DHFR is blocked.

questions.topicName: Topoisomerase, Microtubule Inhibitors, and Antitumor Antibiotics
questions.stem: This schematic contrasts the enzymatic mechanisms of the two DNA-relaxing enzymes shown on the left and on the right. What is the key mechanistic difference between them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The left enzyme requires ATP, while the right enzyme cuts a single strand without energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: The left enzyme adds nucleotides while the right enzyme removes them

choices.label: C
choices.text: The left enzyme cleaves only one DNA strand, while the right enzyme cleaves both strands and requires ATP

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both enzymes cleave double strands, but only the right one is reversible

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both enzymes cut a single strand, but only the left one needs ATP

explanation.summary: Topoisomerase I (left) nicks and religates a single strand and needs no ATP; topoisomerase II (right) cleaves both strands, passes a duplex through the break, and requires ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topoisomerase I (left) nicks and religates a single strand and needs no ATP; topoisomerase II (right) cleaves both strands, passes a duplex through the break, and requires ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the true roles; topoisomerase I (left) cuts a single strand without ATP, while topoisomerase II (right) needs ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Topoisomerases neither add nor remove nucleotides; they cut and reseal DNA to relieve supercoiling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only topoisomerase II cleaves both strands, and both enzymes reseal their breaks, so reversibility does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only topoisomerase I cuts a single strand, and it does not need ATP; topoisomerase II cuts both strands using ATP.
